cells.tense: Endings are arriving by felt necessity right now, and the renewal behind them is being trusted.
cells.act: adjust the share until it is fair, then stop
cells.ask: Find an arrangement where the two sides have drifted — a cost, a standing favor, a recurring effort — set it level once, then keep your hands off it and see whether it holds.
cells.core:
Things are finishing around you because they are finished, not because you cut them off, and that is why the clearing feels clean instead of sharp. You can sense in a thing whether it has run its course, and you move on that sense rather than on the calendar or on someone else's timeline. What comes after the ending is already arriving.

That same even eye works on exchanges. Where a share has drifted, you feel the tilt before you sit down to figure it out. Test it on something small: a household split, a favor you keep covering, an effort that keeps landing on one side. Set the balance right, once, honestly, and then stop adjusting. The point is the proportion you leave standing, not a habit of correcting.
cells.sheetLine: You can tell what is finished, and you let it finish.
cells.verb: letting what has finished end, so what is next can arrive
cells.place: at the still point where what matters shows itself before you can say why

cells.tense: Before this ending has taught you anything, the next one will already be declared.
cells.act: sit with someone in it without fixing it
cells.ask: Before you call the next ending, spend ten minutes with someone who is in the middle of their own change, and offer no advice, no reasons, no fix — just stay with what they are carrying.
cells.core:
You are clearing faster than things can finish. A situation gets heavy, an exit appears, and taking it feels like honesty. From where you sit it reads as freedom; from where those near you sit, the furniture keeps moving. The next ending is often chosen before the current one has taught you what it had to teach.

What is missing is not less change, it is contact. Sitting with someone who is also mid-change, and not managing their process, brings you back near the floor. Their upheaval is no threat to your judgment, and you do not have to solve it. Feeling it alongside them — while keeping your own feet — is what tells you whether this ending is real or rehearsed.
cells.sheetLine: You are calling endings before they have lived.
cells.verb: letting what has finished end, so what is next can arrive

cells.tense: That door closed already, and you are still standing in the doorway, loyal to the room behind.
cells.act: move toward the thing you want, one step, today
cells.ask: Choose something you want that the old arrangement cannot give you, take a step toward it today — a call, a signup, a message out — and wait until after the step to decide what it means.
cells.core:
Something was over before you noticed, and you keep it running anyway. Holding it takes most of what you have, so from inside it looks like care and from outside it reads as loyalty. The old shape is the room you live in. What has not happened is a single move toward whatever comes next, because the last thing has not been set down.

Your direction runs on feeling, and the feeling still points at the old room. So the repair is not a verdict about what should end — it is a small step toward something you actually want. One move, today, before you have settled whether you mean it. The step itself shows you where your energy is willing to go, which is more reliable than any conclusion you could reach about the past.

cells.tense: An ending is underway right now, and nothing in your week has a label on it yet.
cells.act: give the mess a shape it can be carried in
cells.ask: Take the topic you keep drifting back to lately and give it a shape outside your head — a few lines on a page, a folder, dates — so it sits somewhere you can see it instead of inside you.
cells.core:
Something is at the end of its run, and it is finishing without your hand on it. You might notice the tiredness, a subject that keeps returning, a flatness in something you used to look forward to. None of it has been named as change, so nothing has been made ready. The sense of what matters is there, and it has nowhere to sit.

Build one small container. Take the thing you keep circling — a role, a tie, a decision — and give it a form outside: a page, a folder, a handful of lines with dates. You are the one who made it, and it can sit out there from now on. What is coming apart is already telling you its name; you are only giving that a place to be kept.
